notes.meaning: David's first two sons were born while he ruled in Hebron. Amnon was the oldest, but his life later ended in grief and shame after he committed a terrible sin against his half-sister Tamar. Daniel is called Chileab in the book of Second Samuel, showing that he had two names or a second title meaning he looked like his father.

Absalom and Adonijah were David's next two sons. Both of them broke their father's heart by rebelling and trying to take the royal crown for themselves. Absalom's mother was a foreign princess from Geshur, reflecting how kings back then formed political alliances through marriage.

David's fifth and sixth sons born in Hebron were Shephatiah and Ithream. Very little is known about them in the rest of the Bible, but God preserved their names in the royal records. Calling Eglah David's wife balances the list and rounds out the account of the mothers in Hebron.

David reigned over the single tribe of Judah in Hebron for seven and a half years before ruling all twelve tribes from Jerusalem for thirty-three years. Moving the capital to Jerusalem united the nation under God's chosen king. This summary connects the sons born during David's early struggles with those born during his peak years in Jerusalem.

Four sons were born to David and Bathsheba after he made Jerusalem his capital. Solomon is named last even though he became the next king and carried the royal line down to Jesus in Matthew's Gospel. Nathan is also crucial because the Gospel of Luke traces the family line of Jesus through him.

Nine more sons were born to David in Jerusalem by other wives. Some names appear twice in the family, which likely means two older sons died in childhood and later boys were given the same names to honor them. Names like Eliphelet, meaning God is deliverance, show David's deep trust in God during his reign.

David had other sons by concubines, but their names were not recorded in this official royal registry. Tamar is the only daughter listed because her tragic story of mistreatment was a well-known part of the family history. Privilege and power could not protect David's family from the painful results of human sin.

The line of kings from Solomon began with Rehoboam, whose stubbornness caused the kingdom of Israel to split in two. The crown then passed steadily to Abijah, Asa, and Jehoshaphat. God kept His covenant with David by protecting this line of kings generation after generation.

The royal succession continued from Joram to Ahaziah, and then to Joash. Queen Athaliah seized the throne by violence for six years during this era, but she is omitted here because she was not a true descendant of David. God guarded young Joash so that the royal line of David would survive.

Amaziah was followed on the throne by his son Azariah, who was then succeeded by Jotham. Azariah is often called Uzziah in other Bible books, since kings frequently went by more than one name. Throughout these reigns, God preserved the crown in a direct line from father to son.

Ahaz turned away from God, but his son Hezekiah was a faithful king who restored true worship to the nation. After Hezekiah, his son Manasseh ruled for many years and led the people into great idolatry. Even when individual kings failed, God remained faithful to His promise that David's house would endure.

Amon lived wickedly and had a very short reign before his son Josiah became king as a young boy. Josiah became one of Judah's greatest rulers, leading a nationwide revival and rediscovering God's law. His death marked the final peaceful era for the kingdom of Judah before foreign empires conquered it.

Josiah had four sons, but the orderly handover of power from father to son ended after his death. Shallum took the throne name Jehoahaz before being dragged away to Egypt, while foreign rulers placed Jehoiakim and Zedekiah on the throne as puppet kings. The oldest son, Johanan, never ruled and likely died young.

Jeconiah succeeded his father Jehoiakim shortly before Babylon conquered Jerusalem and took him away as a prisoner. The Zedekiah named here was either his uncle who ruled after him or a son who died before the kingdom fell. The shift of power among brothers and uncles showed that the glory of David's earthly kingdom was coming to an end.

The word translated captive notes that Jeconiah lived as an exile in Babylon, where his son Shealtiel was born. The prophet Jeremiah had announced that Jeconiah would be childless regarding the throne, meaning none of his physical offspring would rule as king over Judah. Yet God kept the family alive in exile so the lineage leading to the Messiah would continue.

These six men were additional sons or close relatives in Jeconiah's royal household during the captivity. Shenazzar bears a Babylonian name, showing how David's family was forced to live under foreign customs while in exile. Even without a palace or a country, David's descendants remained preserved by God's providence.

Zerubbabel led the Jewish captives home to Jerusalem to rebuild the ruined temple of God. Other Bible verses call him the son of Shealtiel, which usually means Shealtiel died without sons and his brother Pedaiah fathered Zerubbabel to carry on the family name and inheritance. Names of Zerubbabel's children like Jushab-hesed, meaning mercy is restored, show the joyful hope of the returning exiles.

This list tracks branches of David's family who lived after the return from Babylon. Pelatiah and Jeshaiah were grandsons of Zerubbabel who lived around the time of Ezra. Even though David's family no longer held royal power, God faithfully guarded the lineage leading toward Christ.

Shecaniah's family line continues through Shemaiah and his household. The text counts six descendants, which means Shemaiah the father was counted with his five sons, or one name dropped out during copying. Hattush is likely the same family leader who journeyed back from Babylon with Ezra.

Neariah had three sons who kept David's family record going in the generations after the exile. The name Elioenai means my eyes are toward the Lord, reflecting a quiet trust in God when the nation had no king on the throne. Even in ordinary private life, this family held fast to God's ancient covenant.

The chapter closes with the seven sons of Elioenai, bringing the royal family record deep into the post-exilic period. Ancient Jewish teachers saw the name Anani as a hint of the Messiah who would come with the clouds of heaven. Though the earthly throne was lost, this unbroken family line points forward to Jesus, the eternal King.
